hints: Think about what rate actually means in chemistry, how fast reactants are used up and how fast products form.
Statements 1 and 2 are the textbook definitions of rate, one looks from the reactant side and the other from the product side.
For statement 3, ask yourself if gas volume at constant pressure can track how much product has formed over time.
walkthrough:
**Recall What Rate Means**

Rate is simply change in amount or concentration per unit time. As reaction proceeds, reactants fall and products rise.

$$\text{rate} = \frac{\text{change in concentration}}{\text{time}}$$

**Check Statements 1 and 2**

Statement 1 is the classic definition from the reactant view. Statement 2 is the same idea from the product view.

$$\text{rate} = -\frac{\Delta[\text{reactant}]}{\Delta t} = +\frac{\Delta[\text{product}]}{\Delta t}$$

**Check Statement 3**

If a gas is produced, its volume at constant pressure is directly proportional to moles made. So measuring volume increase per unit time is just another way to follow product appearance.

$$V \propto n \text{ (at constant } p, T\text{), so } \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta t} \text{ measures rate}$$

**Combine The Conclusion**

All three statements describe a valid way to follow rate, by reactants disappearing or by products (including gas) appearing. That gives 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct, because 1, 2 and 3 are all valid. Rate can be followed by loss of reactant, gain of product, or by a property proportional to amount such as gas volume at constant pressure.
options.B: Incorrect if this is 1 and 2 only. It wrongly leaves out 3. Students choose this by thinking only concentration changes count, forgetting that gas volume directly tracks moles of gas product.
options.C: Incorrect if this is 2 and 3 only. It wrongly leaves out 1. The decrease in reactant concentration per unit time is the fundamental definition of rate, so it cannot be excluded.
options.D: Incorrect if this is 1 only. It wrongly leaves out 2 and 3. Rate is symmetrical, it can be measured from either side of the equation, and by physical properties linked to amount.
